title: LiteLLM Router: a production LLM gateway's deployment-selection pipeline
purpose: Place each call naming a model group on one healthy deployment of that group, retrying and falling back on failure while staying inside per-deployment quotas and per-caller budgets.

interface.request: an OpenAI-shaped call naming a model group, optionally carrying a 0-255 priority (litellm/scheduler.py:18)
interface.response: the upstream completion plus decision headers x-litellm-model-id / attempted-retries / attempted-fallbacks / response-cost
interface.config: a model_list of deployments plus a routing strategy name; thresholds are environment variables with shipped defaults (litellm/constants.py:11, :70, :76, :129, :132, :449)

model_selection.property: The named model group is honoured by default; an optional pre-routing hook may substitute a different group first, and the shipped online variant scores groups on a weighted quality-and-price objective.
model_selection.guarantee: Without a pre-routing hook the served model is always from the requested group; with one, substitution is unconstrained by any declared equivalence set. The shipped weights are 0.7 quality / 0.3 cost.

placement.property: Six interchangeable placement strategies over the surviving deployments; the default is a weighted random pick by declared weight, rpm or tpm, falling through to a uniform random pick.
placement.guarantee: Placement is a plug-in point, not a fixed policy: shipped alternatives rank by lowest used TPM, lowest mean observed latency over the last 10 samples with a 1 hour TTL, fewest in-flight calls, or lowest static list price.

admission_and_overload.property: When no deployment survives the filters the call is refused immediately with a 429; waiting is opt-in and only happens if the caller supplied a priority.
admission_and_overload.guarantee: Refusal is instant and explicit rather than silent. The optional queue polls a priority heap every 30 ms until the router timeout expires and then raises a timeout, so a queued request is never silently dropped.

rate_limit_pacing.property: Per-deployment request and token counters keyed to the wall-clock minute: the request count is incremented BEFORE the call in the pre-call check, while tokens are charged only AFTER the call from the real usage figures.
rate_limit_pacing.guarantee: Request pacing is pre-emptive and therefore safe; token pacing is retrospective and therefore always at least one call behind, so a single very large request can overshoot the token quota. A request count is consumed even by an attempt that then fails.

retry_and_fallback.property: Two layers: in-group retries on other deployments first, then up to five cross-group fallback hops. The back-off is zero when a healthy sibling deployment exists, otherwise the server's own Retry-After when it is in (0,60] s, otherwise exponential with jitter.
retry_and_fallback.guarantee: Failover to a different target is preferred over waiting on the same one. Retries are NOT gated on idempotency, and the retry predicate re-issues even after an authentication failure whenever the group has more than one deployment.

outage_and_health.property: A failing deployment is quarantined for a fixed period on evidence of failure: one rejection is enough in a multi-deployment group, otherwise it takes a majority-failure rate over a minimum traffic volume.
outage_and_health.guarantee: Default quarantine is 5 s, the failure-rate threshold is 50% over at least 5 requests in the minute, and a single-deployment group needs a total wipeout over at least 1000 requests. Surprising: when EVERY deployment is quarantined and health-check routing is configured with an explicit allowed-fails policy, the quarantine filter is deliberately bypassed and a known-bad deployment is served.

deadline_and_priority.property: not decided as a deadline: there is no notion of time-remaining or slack anywhere. The only ordering primitive is an optional caller-supplied 0-255 priority.
deadline_and_priority.guarantee: A high-priority request is dequeued first, but nothing relates the wait to any deadline and a request can wait until the router timeout regardless of how much time it had.

tenant_isolation.property: Sliding-window request and token quotas per key, team, user, organisation, end-user, tag and model, over a 60 s window, plus team-based filtering of which deployments a caller may reach.
tenant_isolation.guarantee: It bounds what any one caller may CONSUME; it reserves nothing, so a quota-compliant caller can still be starved by another quota-compliant caller when the shared fleet saturates.

cost_control.property: Hard spend caps per provider, deployment and tag remove over-budget candidates before the call, using spend accumulated after previous calls; separately, a lowest-price placement strategy ranks on a STATIC price table.
cost_control.guarantee: The cap is enforced pre-call against post-call accounting, so it can overshoot by the in-flight calls. Surprising: a model absent from the static price map is priced at 5.0 per token on BOTH input and output, so it sorts last instead of being skipped.

policy_state_and_determinism.property: Stateful and unseeded: the default placement draws from an unseeded random source and the online variant carries per-group posteriors, so two replays of the same traffic do not make the same decisions.
policy_state_and_determinism.guarantee: No reproducibility guarantee at all. Learned state is explicitly bounded (the online variant caps its per-group sample history), but the latency tracker's per-deployment sample buffers expire only on a 1 hour TTL.

decision_observability.property: The decision is returned to the caller in-band as response headers: which deployment served it, how many retries and fallbacks were attempted, what the fallbacks' errors were, and what the call cost.
decision_observability.guarantee: An operator can reconstruct the full attempt chain of any single request from the response alone, without correlating logs.
